subtype: Reading whether an apology is meant [Interpreting]
passage: On Monday Omkar, five, knocked over Hemant's block tower and said "Sorry" quickly, looking at the ceiling. Hemant said "Okay" but kept frowning. On Wednesday Omkar did it again, said "Sorry!" and ran off. Hemant's shoulders dropped. The teacher asked, "Did the sorry fix it?" Hemant shook his head. On Friday Omkar sat down beside him, helped rebuild the tower and said, "Sorry I knocked it. I'll be careful," looking at him. Hemant smiled.

qa.q: What did Omkar do on Friday?
qa.a: He sat beside Hemant, helped rebuild the tower and said sorry while looking at him.

qa.q: Did Hemant believe Omkar's Wednesday apology was meant, and what shows it?
qa.a: No. His shoulders dropped after a quick sorry and Omkar ran off. He might also simply have been disappointed about the tower.

qa.q: How can a teacher help children check whether repair happened?
qa.a: Ask "Did the sorry fix it?" and help them see whether the behaviour stops and something is put right.

qa.q: How might Omkar have experienced saying sorry on Monday?
qa.a: Probably as a quick way to end an awkward moment, without yet knowing how Hemant felt. 🙂

grounding: Shows a child judging apologies by tone, eye contact and whether the behaviour stops, with a teacher helping check repair.

subtype: Reading whether an apology is meant [Interpreting]
passage: At the noisy birthday party, Hansa, five, elbowed Arohi, and Arohi's juice spilled on her dress. "Sorry," Hansa said over her shoulder as she grabbed a balloon. Arohi looked at her dress, then at Hansa's back. "She didn't even look at me," she told her mother. Later Hansa came back holding a napkin. "I'm sorry, I'll be careful," she said in a small voice, looking at the stain and then at Arohi's face. Arohi took it and nodded slowly.

qa.q: What did Hansa hold when she came back?
qa.a: A napkin.

qa.q: Why did Arohi not accept the first sorry?
qa.a: Because Hansa said it over her shoulder without looking at her, so it did not feel meant. She may also just have been upset about her dress.

qa.q: What could Arohi's mother say to help her?
qa.a: Help Arohi name that she felt hurt, and point out that the second apology came with a napkin and eye contact.

qa.q: What might Hansa have felt when she came back with the napkin?
qa.a: Perhaps guilty and wanting to fix it, shown by her small voice and the napkin. She may also have been nervous about being blamed.

grounding: Shows a child judging a sorry by tone and eye contact, and a second apology that comes with repair.

subtype: Reading whether an apology is meant [Interpreting]
passage: In the lobby of their building, a boy grabbed Akash's ball. Akash's mother, Seema, said, “Please give it back.” The boy muttered, “Sorry,” without looking up, and kept holding the ball. Akash said, “He said sorry,” and turned away, though his lip was shaking. Seema knelt. “He said sorry. Did he give the ball back?” Akash looked. “No.” “A real sorry means you stop and fix it.” She turned to the boy. “Please give it back now.” He did. Akash hugged the ball.

qa.q: What did the boy grab?
qa.a: Akash's ball.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when he turned away with his lip shaking?
qa.a: He was upset about his ball and confused, because he accepted the sorry even though nothing changed.

qa.q: What did Seema teach Akash about sorry?
qa.a: That a real sorry means stopping and fixing it, and she helped check whether the ball came back.

qa.q: How might the boy see Seema's second request?
qa.a: He'd learn that saying sorry isn't enough, and that he needed to give the ball back.

grounding: A child accepts a sorry at face value, and his mother helps him check whether repair actually happened.

subtype: Reading whether an apology is meant [Interpreting]
passage:
“Didi, Rohit kicked my chair again.”
“Did you tell him to stop?” asked Sunaina.
“Yes. He said sorry.”
“Did he stop?”
Wasim thought. “No. He kicked it three more times. But he said sorry.”
“Hmm. When someone's really sorry, what do they do?”
“Stop kicking?”
“Yes. How did his sorry sound?”
“Laughy. He wasn't looking at me.”
“So maybe not a real sorry. Tomorrow, if he kicks again, tell your teacher.”
“Okay.” Wasim sighed. “I thought sorry fixed it.”

qa.q: How many more times did Rohit kick the chair after saying sorry?
qa.a: Three more times.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when he sighed?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and a bit confused, having believed that sorry fixed things.

qa.q: How did Sunaina help Wasim judge the sorry?
qa.a: She asked whether Rohit stopped, how the sorry sounded and whether he looked at him, so Wasim could see it wasn't real.

qa.q: What is it like for Wasim to keep getting kicked after a sorry?
qa.a: It is confusing and frustrating, because the word promised a fix that didn't come.

grounding: A preschooler accepts a sorry at face value, and his sister helps him check tone, eye contact and whether the behaviour stopped.

subtype: Reading whether an apology is meant [Interpreting]
passage:
Note by Vandana, KG teacher.
Today a boy snatched Deepak's crayons. When I stepped in, the boy said “sorry” quickly while looking out of the window, and then grabbed another crayon. Deepak said, “It's okay,” and smiled. I asked Deepak, “Did he stop?” Deepak shook his head. I asked the boy to look at Deepak and give the crayon back. He did, and this time his sorry was quiet and he looked at him. Deepak said, “That one was real.” We'll keep practising what sorry means.

qa.q: Where was the boy looking when he first said sorry?
qa.a: Out of the window.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when he said “It's okay” and smiled?
qa.a: He probably felt he should accept any sorry, even though he was upset about his crayons.

qa.q: What did Vandana do to help Deepak check the repair?
qa.a: Vandana asked if the boy had stopped and guided the boy to look at Deepak and give the crayon back.

qa.q: How might the boy feel when asked to look at Deepak and give the crayon back?
qa.a: He may feel a bit embarrassed, but he learns that a real sorry means stopping and giving back.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a preschooler accepting any sorry at face value and being helped to check whether repair happened.

subtype: Reading whether an apology is meant [Interpreting]
passage:
Under the big tree in the hill village, the children were queueing for the rope swing. Lalremsiami pushed in front of Bidisha, knocking her sideways.

"Say sorry," someone called.

"Sorry," Lalremsiami muttered, grinning at her friends, and didn't move.

"Okay," said Bidisha, and stood behind her.

Bidisha's Nani, sorting beans on her porch, called her over. "Did she mean that sorry?"

Bidisha shrugged. "She said it."

"Look. Is she giving your turn back?"

Bidisha looked. Lalremsiami was already swinging. "No."

"Then it isn't fixed yet. Let's go and talk to them together."

qa.q: What was Bidisha's Nani sorting on her porch?
qa.a: Beans.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling when she said "Okay" and stood behind?
qa.a: She probably felt a bit hurt at being pushed, but accepted the "sorry" at face value, trusting that the word fixed things. Her shrug suggests she was unsure what else to expect.

qa.q: How did Nani help Bidisha check whether repair had happened?
qa.a: She asked Bidisha to look at whether Lalremsiami gave the turn back, so Bidisha could see the behaviour hadn't changed, and then offered to talk to them together.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami treat the apology?
qa.a: She treats it as a word to get out of trouble: she mutters it while grinning at her friends and keeps the turn.

grounding: It shows a young child accepting a "sorry" at face value and an adult helping her check tone and whether the behaviour stopped.
